title: Wren and the Smile
premise: Oscar Vasquez, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week—each humming fragments of an old lullaby that ends mid-verse. When photographs from their late grandmother's house start showing an extra chair at every table, Oscar and their found family of insomniac callers realize the song is a summons, and the chair is being set for one of them. The entity behind it is the town's long-buried debt: a century of deaths ruled accidents by men who profited from them. To end it, Oscar must broadcast the song's final verse—a verse that names the guilty and frees the dead—but singing along with it means joining them. In the climax, Oscar lets the frost take their voice instead, broadcasting the verse in silence while the family speaks it aloud together; the dead are released, the guilty are named on air, and the extra chair finally appears empty.
about_author: Cyrus Brightwater is the pen name of a former small-town radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining transmitter towers in frost-prone valleys before turning to fiction. They write horror about grief, documentation, and the things that answer when you talk into the dark.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. During a routine overnight shift, Oscar takes a call from Marisol, a devoted listener—and learns she died six days ago. She hums four bars of a lullaby before the line drops. The emotional beat is uncanny denial: Oscar documents the call obsessively, telling themselves it's a prank, while the studio clock refuses to move past 3:33.

chapters.title: The Listeners Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Three more dead callers phone in over successive nights, each humming the same incomplete melody. Oscar reaches out to two living regulars—Dee, a retired nurse, and Kofi, a night-shift baker—who form a wary listening circle. Beat: tentative found-family warmth shadowed by dread, as the group realizes the callers only ever ask one question: 'Did they find out yet?'

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Dee inherits her grandmother's house and finds boxes of photographs: every image, across sixty years, shows an extra wooden chair at the table—newer photos show it closer. In the back of a hymnal, sheet music titled 'The Frost Verse,' missing its last page. Beat: creeping violation; home itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: What the Town Buried
chapters.summary: Kofi's POV. Researching the lullaby, Kofi uncovers the Hollis Mill collapse of 1924: eleven workers killed, ruled accidental, compensation pocketed by the founding families—including Dee's grandmother's employers. The dead callers all descend from mill families. Beat: righteous anger crystallizing into purpose; justice outside the law becomes the group's shared creed.

chapters.title: Signal Bleed
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The station manager orders Oscar to stop taking 'crank calls'; that night the transmitter broadcasts the lullaby on its own, citywide, and every phone in town rings once. The extra chair now appears in Oscar's own apartment photos, positioned facing the radio. Beat: loss of control—the story stops being something Oscar documents and starts documenting them.

chapters.title: The Verse That Names
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. A dying archivist, one of the callers, explains the mechanism: the song was written by mill widows as a curse ledger, each verse naming a guilty family; the last verse was never sung because the final name was never spoken aloud. Whoever completes it binds or banishes the debt. Beat: revelation and terrible choice—knowledge arrives with a price tag.

chapters.title: Frost Patterns
chapters.summary: Kofi's POV. Winter closes in. Frost ferns spread across windows spelling names—first the guilty, then, chillingly, the listeners' own. One of the circle, Ruthie, answers the song's call and is found seated in the extra chair, smiling, frozen. Beat: devastating midpoint loss; grief fuses the remaining trio into true family.

chapters.title: The Men Who Profited
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The descendants of the founding families, led by councilman Aldous Merrick, try to buy and demolish the station, then threaten the trio directly—revealing they've known about the song for generations and have been feeding it substitutes. Beat: cold fury; the horror doubles as the human villains prove worse than the ghost.

chapters.title: Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, intercut with all voices. On the anniversary night, the trio seizes the station as Merrick's men close in. Oscar begins reading the final verse on air—but the song demands a voice be given to the frost. Oscar opens their mouth to sing along and feels the cold take hold. Beat: climax at full pitch; sacrifice chosen in real time.

chapters.title: Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Dee's POV, weeks later. Oscar survives voiceless, communicating through typed notes and the sign language Kofi teaches everyone. The broadcast named the guilty; investigations reopen; the frost patterns fade. In the last photograph of the three of them at Dee's table, there are four chairs—and no one sitting in the fourth. Beat: bittersweet resolution; the family remains, the debt is paid, and silence becomes a kind of prayer answered.
